title: A Technical Note on Keeping Build Pipelines Boring
summary: Why I'd rather have a build script I can read top to bottom in five minutes than a clever framework I have to look up every time.
body:
Every time I evaluate a new static site generator, I end up asking the same question: could I explain exactly what this does to another engineer in five minutes? For most of the popular options, the honest answer is no — there's a plugin system, a config resolution order, and a handful of "magic" conventions to memorize first.

## Boring on purpose

For this site, the entire pipeline is a handful of plain Node scripts:

- Read and validate JSON content against a schema
- Render Markdown to sanitized HTML
- Stamp the result into a couple of HTML templates with simple curly-brace token substitution
- Write files to `dist/`

That's it. No plugin ecosystem, no build cache to invalidate, no config DSL. When something breaks, I can read the whole thing in one sitting and know exactly where to look.

## Validation at the boundary

The part I care about most isn't the templating, it's validating content *before* anything gets rendered. Every article is checked against a JSON Schema before the build touches it, so a malformed date or a missing required field fails loudly and immediately instead of producing a broken page somewhere in `dist/`.

```
content (JSON) → schema validation → markdown → sanitize → templates → dist/
```

## The takeaway

**Boring technology is a feature, not a compromise.** A pipeline you fully understand is one you can actually trust, and trust matters more than cleverness for something as low-stakes and long-lived as a personal blog.
author: Charlie Cunningham
